items.title: [stirileprotv.ro] Researchers identify possible largest known scorpion, over one meter long
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Researchers have identified Praearcturus gigas, a scorpion known from a fossil found in the United Kingdom dating to about 415 million years ago, as a candidate for the largest known scorpion. They estimated that the animal exceeded one meter in length. A new analysis combining CT scans with traditional fossil tracings resolved decades of uncertainty over its classification. Paleontologist Richie Howard and colleagues infer that it hunted both on land and in water; terrestrial ecosystems were still developing at the time. The researchers suggest that the absence of other large predators may have enabled its large size, while later competition may have contributed to its decline.

items.title: [theconversation.com] Global temperatures exceed pre-industrial average by 2°C for a week as El Niño intensifies
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Preliminary data from Copernicus, the European Union’s climate-monitoring service, show global temperatures stayed more than 2°C above the 1850–1900 average for seven consecutive days, reaching 2.25°C above that baseline on Monday. These daily readings do not establish that the Paris Agreement’s temperature limit has been breached: that target is assessed over at least 20 years. Scientists attribute the spike to long-term human-caused warming combined with a strong El Niño. The record run coincided with COP31 climate negotiations in Turkey, where nearly 200 countries failed to agree on language about moving away from fossil fuels. The UK Met Office forecasts an unusually sharp rise in atmospheric carbon dioxide in 2027 as drought weakens natural carbon sinks; one estimate puts the year-to-year increase at about 3.5 parts per million. The current El Niño began in June and is expected to continue until at least March.

items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Floodwaters have peaked across much of Vancouver Island and British Columbia’s south coast, but river levels remain a serious concern on central Vancouver Island after days of rain, high tides and storm surge. The provincial River Forecast Centre issued a flood warning for central Island waterways, where rivers had reached their banks or were expected to overflow soon. Officials said eastern Vancouver Island remained under a flood watch and coastal flood warnings continued in many areas. Courtenay declared a local emergency and ordered evacuations from several low-lying properties, including the Maple Pool campground, while the Regional District of Nanaimo ordered some Cedar residents to leave homes along the Nanaimo River. Rain and wind warnings for the South Coast were lifted Thursday, but officials said rivers would need time to recede before advisories could be withdrawn. The Effingham Island weather station recorded 469 millimetres of rain in just over two days.

items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

France’s public agricultural research institute INRAE plans to build an AI assistant using verified scientific data to help farmers respond to climate change and other pressures. The project awaits approval for €1.2 million in France 2030 funding, with a first version planned for farmer testing within 18 months. Separately, John Deere expanded access to its free JD assistant on Nov. 16, linking it to the company’s Operations Center farm-management platform. INRAE’s proposed assistant would tailor guidance to a farm’s location, practices, soil, expected water resources and finances, while Deere’s tool searches and analyzes information already recorded about a user’s fields, machinery and farm operations. INRAE says the project has demonstrated answers to simple queries and aims to handle more complex questions; farmer testing depends on the funding decision.

items.title: [grist.org] Michigan court leaves state renewable energy siting rules largely intact
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The Michigan Supreme Court declined to hear a challenge by dozens of townships to Public Act 233, the 2023 law that lets the state approve certain renewable energy projects when local zoning rules exceed the law’s standards. The order leaves most of that framework in place, but the court also ruled that any local government affected by a project—not only the government with zoning authority—can qualify as an affected local unit. The justices have not resolved a separate dispute over when a 30-day deadline begins for local officials to tell developers they have a qualifying ordinance. They scheduled arguments for the January 2027 session and directed the parties to file briefs in December and January. The order does not approve or reject any specific energy project.

items.title: [physicsworld.com] Scientists propose supercritical fluids drove deep Mariana volcanic eruptions
items.content_html:

items.title: [efeagro.com] European farmers protest subsidy cuts as EU budget summit fails
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

European farmers protested in Brussels on Nov. 26 against proposed cuts to the European Union’s Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) as leaders debated the bloc’s 2028-34 budget. The European Council summit ended without agreement, and its planned second day was canceled. Talks are due to resume at a Dec. 17-18 summit. Farm groups say the latest budget plans could cut CAP funding by more than 20% after inflation. They also oppose folding agricultural and regional support into broader national plans, which they fear would give governments greater discretion over allocations. European Council President António Costa’s Nov. 21 compromise proposal put the overall EU budget at €1.582 trillion, below the European Commission’s original €1.76 trillion plan. Farmers’ organizations estimate the CAP reduction at about 15% in nominal terms and more after inflation. CAP funding supports farm income, rural development and environmental measures. Spain’s COAG farm organization estimates the proposed changes could reduce Spanish farm income by €877.5 million annually, while Dutch agriculture organization LTO says the plans put nearly a quarter of the Netherlands’ CAP allocation at risk. Farm group Copa-Cogeca has called farmers back to Brussels on Dec. 17 for a larger tractor-led demonstration alongside the next budget summit.

COP31 negotiations in Antalya continued past their scheduled Friday close as representatives of climate-vulnerable countries pressed for firm funding commitments to prepare for worsening climate impacts. The summit’s nearly 200 countries remained divided over a political agreement, including whether it should call for a transition away from fossil fuels. Ghana’s Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings, who leads the African negotiating group, said public adaptation funding from developed countries totaled $28.2 billion to $31.7 billion in 2024, compared with an estimated need of about $305 billion annually by 2035. The revised draft offered no detailed commitments on the issue; a report is expected before the 2027 climate conference in Ethiopia. Pacific island representatives also pointed to a funding shortfall for climate resilience: the Pacific Resilience Facility remained about $300 million short of its $500 million goal after a summit event drew just one new offer, $5 million from Australian mining executive and philanthropist Andrew Forrest. At a late Friday plenary, delegates approved technical decisions but left the main political text unresolved. COP31 President Murat Kurum said a new draft was expected Saturday.

items.title: [phys.org] Neolithic tomb pots point to fermented milk offerings in Denmark
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Researchers studying 330 Neolithic pots from western Zealand, Denmark, found corrosion on 31; 29 came from passage tombs. In experiments with reconstructed vessels, fresh, unpasteurized milk produced damage resembling the marks on ancient pottery, while beer and mead did not. The findings, published in Antiquity, suggest fermented dairy may have been placed with the dead, although corrosion alone cannot identify the contents with certainty. The results challenge an earlier interpretation that the corroded pots held beer, an idea based partly on evidence from brewing communities elsewhere. Fermentation makes milk more acidic, and the researchers say fermented dairy products could also have been easier to digest and lasted longer. Lead author Lone Claudi-Hansen, an archaeologist, said she hopes to examine pottery from other parts of Denmark to see whether the same pattern appears elsewhere.

items.title: [openai.com] Cisco and OpenAI release Linux shield to block exploits during patching
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Networking company Cisco and artificial intelligence company OpenAI released Shirudo on Nov. 23, an open-source tool designed to protect Linux systems temporarily while teams test and deploy permanent software fixes. Attackers may exploit newly disclosed vulnerabilities before organizations can test and install patches across their systems. Shirudo uses AI agents and Linux’s eBPF technology to develop and test targeted “shields.” Security teams can check whether a shield blocks vulnerable behavior without interrupting legitimate service, then approve it for deployment. They can remove the protection once they install a permanent patch. In a controlled demonstration, a shield generated with OpenAI’s Codex coding agent blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without a restart. Cisco and OpenAI also cited testing against a PHP vulnerability. The companies have invited developers, researchers and infrastructure operators to contribute and scheduled a technical webinar for Dec. 15.

The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), the U.N. nuclear watchdog, is negotiating with Russia and Ukraine for a ninth localized ceasefire around the Russian-held Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant after it lost its connection to its last remaining external power line on Nov. 25, reportedly due to military activity. The IAEA also says another key supply route, the Dniprovska 750-kilovolt line and substation, needs further work.

items.title: [phys.org] Cosmology researchers test rival accounts of dark energy and cosmic expansion
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Researchers have proposed two different explanations for dark energy, the component estimated to make up about 70% of the universe’s energy. A team from the University of British Columbia and the University of Sheffield says quantum chromodynamics (QCD)—the established theory of the strong nuclear force—could account for the observed acceleration of cosmic expansion through properties of the quantum vacuum, without requiring a new particle or field. The team found that its model fit observations of supernovae and early-universe radiation about as well as standard cosmological models. Separately, a University of Ottawa study tested a model called CCC+TL, which attributes effects usually assigned to dark matter and dark energy to changing physical constants and “tired light.” The researchers say it matched several observations, including light-element abundances and cosmic-chronometer measurements. The model also estimates the universe is 26.7 billion years old. Both proposals remain theoretical, and the QCD team plans to test its calculations against future space-telescope data.

Germany’s BSI and security experts urged organizations to strengthen basic defenses, including incident response, access controls and network separation.

items.title: [scientificamerican.com] Neanderthal DNA variant linked to smaller visual brain region, lower schizophrenia odds
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Researchers report that a Neanderthal-derived DNA variant is associated with a smaller occipital lobe and lower odds of schizophrenia in modern humans. In UK Biobank data, each copy of the variant corresponded to about 0.85 cubic centimeters less occipital-lobe volume; people with two copies had nearly 10% lower odds of schizophrenia than those with no copies. The occipital lobe processes visual information. The variant lies near DAAM1, a gene involved in brain development, but researchers have not established how it affects the brain or whether the smaller lobe explains the schizophrenia association. The variant was not associated with a meaningful difference in intelligence, and outside researchers cautioned against drawing conclusions about Neanderthal brain function from the findings in modern humans. The study was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Its authors say further work, including studies using brain organoids or animal models, could investigate the mechanism.

Investigators have linked the communications overload behind Friday’s nationwide U.S. flight halt to a recently installed router at a Federal Aviation Administration radio facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, according to a Wall Street Journal investigation. The disruption affected 17 of the FAA’s 22 en-route centers after initial communication glitches appeared at its Indianapolis center. items.content_html:

The U.N. Security Council unanimously renewed the mandate of its peacekeeping mission in the Central African Republic, known as MINUSCA, through Nov. 15, 2027. The French-drafted resolution, adopted Nov. 12, also adjusts the mission’s priorities. The military troop ceiling falls from 14,046 to 12,000, and the mission will continue supporting security-force deployments, including a pilot garrison-based army, especially in border areas. The resolution directs MINUSCA to continue its work on disarmament and reintegration, human rights and combating impunity as responsibilities gradually shift to national institutions. Liberia’s U.N. ambassador, Lewis Garseedah Brown II, warned that the transition requires resources and that the U.N.’s cash shortage must not hinder the mission. The extension keeps the mission in place for another year, with the next mandate deadline set for Nov. 15, 2027.

items.title: [36kr.com] EU sues IBM, Atos and Leonardo over border system delays
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The European Union has sued IBM, French IT group Atos and Italian defence contractor Leonardo over repeated delays in developing its Entry/Exit System (EES), an electronic border-check system for the 29-country Schengen area. The EU agency eu-LISA filed the civil case in Estonia in December 2025; the dispute became public on Monday. The agency and the European Commission say the case concerns development delays, not the system’s current operation. The system was initially scheduled to launch in 2022 but was not fully rolled out until 2026. Its introduction caused hours-long airport queues after fingerprint scanners malfunctioned, including when exposed to sweat. Some countries are still acquiring scanners. The system records fingerprints and photographs from non-EU travellers on their first entry to help identify visa overstayers and identity fraud. eu-LISA says the case does not affect operations. Estonia’s Harju County Court has accepted the case, but no hearing has been held or scheduled.

items.title: [pewresearch.org] Pew projects Muslims will surpass Christians globally by 2035
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Muslims are projected to become the world’s largest religious group by 2035, reaching 2.57 billion people compared with 2.52 billion Christians, according to new projections from the Pew Research Center. Both populations are expected to grow, but the Muslim population is projected to increase faster, mainly because Muslim women had an average of 3.1 children in 2020-2025, compared with 2.5 among Christian women. Pew estimates there were 2.02 billion Muslims and 2.27 billion Christians in 2020. If current trends continue, the Muslim population will exceed 3.6 billion by 2070, while the Christian population will remain just below 3 billion. The world population is projected to grow 29% over the same period. The report models demographic patterns across 201 countries and territories, including age, fertility, mortality, migration and religious switching. Its projections do not account for events such as wars, epidemics or natural disasters. By 2070, sub-Saharan Africa is expected to be home to more than half of the world’s Christians, while Pakistan is projected to have the largest Muslim population. Pew’s researchers say the projected growth is largely taking place in countries where each faith is already predominant, rather than reflecting a direct shift from one religion to the other.

items._excerpt: Muslims are projected to become the world’s largest religious group by 2035, reaching 2.57 billion people compared with 2.52 billion Christians, according to new projections from the Pew Research Center. Both populations are expected to grow, but the Muslim population is projected to increase faster, mainly because Muslim women had an average of 3.1 children in 2020-2025, compared with 2.5 among Christian women (pewresearch.org, pbs.org). Pew estimates there were 2.02 billion Muslims and 2.27 billion Christians in 2020. If current trends continue, the Muslim population will exceed 3.6 billion by 2070, while the Christian population will remain just below 3 billion. The world population is projected to grow 29% over the same period (pewresearch.org). The report models demographic patterns across 201 countries and territories, including age, fertility, mortality, migration and religious switching. Its projections do not account for events such as wars, epidemics or natural disasters (pewresearch.org). By 2070, sub-Saharan Africa is expected to be home to more than half of the world’s Christians, while Pakistan is projected to have the largest Muslim population (pewresearch.org). Pew’s researchers say the projected growth is largely taking place in countries where each faith is already predominant, rather than reflecting a direct shift from one religion to the other (pewresearch.org, dw.com). Switching patterns: From 2020 to 2070, Pew projects religious switching will result in net losses of 8 million Muslims and 105 million Christians; movement directly between Islam and Christianity is expected to roughly balance (pewresearch.org). African growth: Pew projects sub-Saharan Africa’s Muslim population will rise from about 369 million in 2020 to 980 million in 2070, increasing its share of the world’s Muslims from 18% to 27% (peopledaily.digital). items.title: [ft.com] Italian rail and airport strikes extend disruption after Europe-wide protests
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Italy’s 24-hour strike on Friday disrupted schools, some health services and local transport, while a separate rail stoppage was due to run until 8 p.m. Saturday and airport workers planned walkouts Sunday in Milan and Venice. Travelers faced further disruption from the separate rail and airport strikes. The strike called by the CGIL trade union excluded air and rail transport, and local transit operators had to maintain minimum service. The Italian dispute centers on a proposed €26 billion budget for 2027 that the union says fails to support incomes and public services. Italy’s annual inflation reached 5.5% in October, up from 4.2% in September. Real wages remained below early-2021 levels, and the economy stagnated in the third quarter, the Financial Times reported. The Italian stoppage coincided with coordinated youth demonstrations in more than 25 European countries, with organizers calling for investment in education, housing and welfare rather than military spending. In Switzerland, protests in several cities ended in clashes, while police in Vienna used pepper spray and made arrests after disturbances at a youth rally. Germany’s youth movement said about 87,000 people joined demonstrations nationwide.

items.title: [simon42.com] Home Assistant Beta enables camera recordings with HomeKit Secure Video in Apple Home
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The second beta of the smart home software Home Assistant 2026.12 makes it possible for the first time to connect cameras via the HomeKit Bridge and save their recordings with HomeKit Secure Video in Apple Home. Until now, the Bridge only transmitted live video; additional software was needed for recordings. Requirements include an Apple home hub, an iCloud+ subscription, a motion sensor, and setting up the camera as a standalone HomeKit accessory. Recording must be enabled separately for each camera. Recordings only start when motion is detected. As a result, the first few seconds may be missing. Home Assistant recommends H.264 streams, since conversion via FFmpeg uses processing power. In the developer test, an H.265 source failed to meet the Apple home hub’s time limit. The final version is planned for December 2, 2026; until then, beta features may still change.
